key_insight: In a Vanderbilt EHR review, a small but distinct group of psychosis patients had AI-related interactions that appeared to worsen or shape symptoms, especially after ChatGPT became widely available.
clinical_relevance: The findings suggest clinicians should consider recent AI use when assessing psychosis presentations, particularly in first-episode cases where AI may amplify delusional thinking.
method: Searched Vanderbilt University Medical Center EHR notes for AI-related keywords from 12/1/2022 to 4/1/2026.
Included records only when the primary diagnosis involved psychosis and the note content was judged AI-related.
Three raters classified cases into four interaction types: Catalyst, Amplifier, Co-Author, or Object.
evidence_signal: Of 73 qualifying patients, 28 were rated as AI psychosis, 17 had neutral AI interactions, and 28 had AI-themed delusions without documented conversational AI use; 60.7% of AI psychosis cases were first-episode psychosis.
watch_item: This is a single-center retrospective EHR study, so note documentation may miss AI use and the findings may not generalize beyond one academic medical setting.
paper_title: Characterizing artificial intelligence (AI) psychosis in a large academic medical setting: evidence of the new clinical phenomenon and the vulnerability of those in early phases of psychosis
